                                   1                                        II.      DISCUSSION

                                   2   A.     Legal Standard

                                   3          As noted above, the Bank has moved to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction pursuant

                                   4   to Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(2). The Bank has also moved to dismiss for improper

                                   5   venue under Rule 12(b)(3) and for failure to state a claim for relief under Rule 12(b)(6).

                                   6           “When a defendant moves to dismiss for lack of personal jurisdiction, ‘the plaintiff bears

                                   7   the burden of demonstrating that jurisdiction is appropriate.’” Morrill v. Scott Fin. Corp., 873

                                   8   F.3d 1136, 1141 (9th Cir. 2017). If no evidentiary hearing is held, the plaintiff need only make a

                                   9   prima facie showing that there is personal jurisdiction. See id. “All uncontroverted allegations in

                                  10   the complaint are deemed true, and factual disputes are to be resolved in favor of the non-moving

                                  11   party.” Id.

                                  12           “Similar to a motion to dismiss [for lack of personal jurisdiction] under Rule 12(b)(2), ‘the
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   plaintiff bears the burden of showing that venue is proper.’” Cadence Design Sys. v. Yunjing

                                  14   Intelligent Innovation Shenzhen Co., No. 25-cv-00317-AMO, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 55917, at

                                  15   *10 (N.D. Cal. Mar. 17, 2026). Implicitly, a venue challenge – similar to a personal jurisdiction

                                  16   challenge – can be facial or factual in nature. See Meyers v. Autodesk, Inc., No. 4:22-CV-00074-

                                  17   LPR, 2022 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 184227, at *3 (E.D. Ark. Oct. 7, 2022); Marquardt v. Blue Jay

                                  18   Transit, Inc., No. 2:26-cv-00444-CAS-SKx, 2026 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 62331, at *16 (C.D. Cal. Mar.

                                  19   23, 2026). Likewise, implicitly, for a factual challenge, a plaintiff need only make out a prima

                                  20   facie case of venue. See id.

                                  21          Finally, "[t]o survive a motion to dismiss for failure to state a claim after the Supreme

                                  22   Court's decisions in Iqbal and Twombly, [a plaintiff’s] allegations must suggest that [its] claim has

                                  23   at least a plausible chance of success." Levitt v. Yelp! Inc., 765 F.3d 1123, 1134-35 (9th Cir. 2014)

                                  24   (internal quotation marks omitted). The court must assume the plaintiff’s allegations are true and

                                  25   draw all reasonable inferences in their favor. See Shields v. Credit One Bank, N.A., 32 F.4th 1218,

                                  26   1220 (9th Cir. 2022).

                                   5                   which the district court sits. Because California's long-arm
                                                       jurisdictional statute is coextensive with federal due process
                                   6                   requirements, the jurisdictional analyses under state law and federal
                                                       due process are the same. For a court to exercise personal
                                   7                   jurisdiction over a nonresident defendant, that defendant must have
                                                       at least "minimum contacts" with the relevant forum such that the
                                   8                   exercise of jurisdiction "does not offend traditional notions of fair
                                                       play and substantial justice."

                                  20   investor case and the transfer agent case into two different fora. The Court is not unsympathetic to

                                  21   that point. However, multiple cases can arise where there are (as alleged) multiple tortfeasors or

                                  22   multiple acts affecting multiple parties. Furthermore, there are also tools to deal with

                                  23   inefficiencies that may arise from the litigation of two related cases, including but not limited to

                                  24   coordination of discovery, stays, and possible transfer of venue.

                                  25   C.      Request to Take Jurisdictional Discovery

                                  26           Equiniti argues that, even if there is no personal jurisdiction based on the record presented,

                                  27   it should be allowed to take jurisdictional discovery to assess whether there could be personal

                                  28   jurisdiction.
                                                                                         21
                                        Case 3:25-cv-01853-EMC             Document 65         Filed 05/01/26     Page 22 of 23




                                   1           District courts have discretion in deciding whether to permit jurisdictional discovery.

                                   2                   Jurisdictional discovery "should ordinarily be granted where
                                                       pertinent facts bearing on the question of jurisdiction are
                                   3                   controverted or where a more satisfactory showing of the facts is
                                                       necessary." But "a mere hunch that discovery might yield
                                   4                   jurisdictionally relevant facts, or bare allegations in the face of
                                                       specific denials, are insufficient reasons for a court to grant
                                   5                   jurisdictional discovery." "The district court's refusal to provide
                                                       such discovery will not be reversed except upon the clearest
                                   6                   showing that denial of discovery results in actual and substantial
                                                       prejudice to the complaining litigant."
                                   7

                                   8   Yamashita v. LG Chem, Ltd., 62 F.4th 496, 507 (9th Cir. 2023).

                                   9           In its papers, Equiniti identifies discovery that it would like to take. See Mot. at 18-19.

                                  10   Much of that discovery, however, is related to general jurisdiction which, as noted above, Equiniti

                                  11   largely conceded at the hearing does not exist.

                                  12           At the hearing, Equiniti did argue that it should be allowed to take discovery into whether
Northern District of California
 United States District Court




                                  13   the Bank knew its guarantees could affect California investors. However, that information is

                                  14   irrelevant. It is predicated on Equiniti’s position that specific jurisdiction can be based on a

                                  15   stream-of-commerce theory, but the Court has already rejected that position. Cf. Yamashita, 62

                                  16   F.4th at 507 (“Given our analysis of specific personal jurisdiction, most of the information [the

                                  17   plaintiff] seeks is clearly irrelevant . . . .”). Equiniti has not asked for any discovery (to support

                                  18   specific jurisdiction) tied to the transaction at issue. Moreover, Equiniti has not made any

                                  19   allegations or provided any evidence even suggesting that the Bank knew or should have known

                                  20   about any connection that the SM Trust had to California and that it purposefully directed its

                                  21   conduct at California, even though Equiniti is located in New York or Minnesota. See id. at 508

                                  22   (“Jurisdictional discovery would be little more than a fishing expedition seeking support for

                                  23   jurisdictional theories one of which is farfetched . . . .”).

                                  24                                         III.      CONCLUSION

                                  25           For the foregoing reasons, the Court grants the Bank’s motion to dismiss based on lack of

                                  26   personal jurisdiction. There is no general jurisdiction, consent jurisdiction, or specific jurisdiction

                                  27   over the Bank. Furthermore, Equiniti has not demonstrated that jurisdictional discovery could

                                  28   uncover any material information that would change the result.
                                                                                           22
                                        Case 3:25-cv-01853-EMC           Document 65        Filed 05/01/26      Page 23 of 23




                                   1          Because the Court is dismissing Equiniti’s claims against the Bank for lack of personal

                                   2   jurisdiction, it does not entertain the other arguments made by the Bank in its motion – e.g., that

                                   3   venue is not proper or that Equiniti has failed to state a claim for relief. Although the Court is

                                   4   dismissing all of Equiniti’s claims against the Bank, its ruling here does not preclude Equiniti

                                   5   from filing a new suit against the Bank in a different court.

                                   6          This order disposes of Docket No. 55.

                                   7

                                   8          IT IS SO ORDERED.
